entry.title: Chuquimamani-Condori Shares Some Kelela Edits After Their C2C Reunion
entry.summary: After reuniting with Kelela at Italian dance festival C2C, Chuquimamani-Condori has shared edits of Kelela songs available for download.
entry.content:
2025 may have been the year of Chuquimamani-Condori, but 2026 has been pretty good on that front too. In addition to the wonderful Wak'a EP from Los Thuthanaka, Chuquimamani-Condori's duo with their brother Joshua Chuquimia Crampton, we've also gotten some new DJ E edits. Today, we're getting even more.

Chuquimamani-Condori collaborated with Kelela on a decade ago on the tracks "Final Exam" and "Reference Track" for the 2016 Berlin Biennale. More recently, they included some Kelela edits on their Turn mix for NTS last month, and it seems there's plenty where those came from.

After reuniting with Kelela at long-running Italian dance music festival C2C a few weeks ago, Chuquimamani-Condori has taken to Instagram to share a Mediafire link containing eight edits of Kelela songs. "Sharing some Kelela edits from old dj sets over the years - this is my ayni to you Kelela, an unpayable debt for your generosity," they wrote. Download them here.

entry.title: Ambrose Kenny-Smith & O.R.B. Announce Debut Album As ORBROSE: Hear “Lightweight”
entry.summary: King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's Ambrose Kenny-Smith has teamed up with fellow Australian psych-rockers O.R.B. as ORBROSE.
entry.content:
King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's Ambrose Kenny-Smith and O.R.B.'s Zak Olsen are longtime friends, kindred spirits, and fellow Aussie psych-rock travelers. By their powers combined, they are ORBROSE.

ORBROSE, the team-up of Kenny-Smith, Olsen, and the latter's O.R.B. bandmates John Zacharias and Daff Gravolin, are releasing their self-titled collection of classic bluesy rock and '70s-inspired Australian boogie in March. Today, they're giving us a taste by sharing lead single "Lightweight."

The track "began with Ambrose's harmonica riff," they explain. "This one really came together so easily and quickly. I can remember all of us laughing when it kicked in for the first time 'cause it sounded so cool. It’s an ode to all the old barflies that used to hang around our local pub in Geelong (The Nash), where we all grew up together playing in bands." Listen below.

entry.title: When We Were Young Announces 2027 Lineup With Blink-182, Limp Bizkit, Third Eye Blind, & More
entry.summary: When it properly got going in 2022 (after a one-off incarnation in 2017), the Las Vegas music festival When We Were Young tapped into a fertile market: nostalgia for Warped Tour-era pop-punk, emo, and metalcore. WWWY remained a popular destination for aging MySpace users for several years, but the fest skipped 2026, raising concerns about…
entry.content:
When it properly got going in 2022 (after a one-off incarnation in 2017), the Las Vegas music festival When We Were Young tapped into a fertile market: nostalgia for Warped Tour-era pop-punk, emo, and metalcore. WWWY remained a popular destination for aging MySpace users for several years, but the fest skipped 2026, raising concerns about its future despite assurances from organizers that it would return in 2027. They kept their word: When We Were Young is coming back next year, and they've got the lineup to prove it.

Like so many festivals that begin with a tightly defined aesthetic, When We Were Young seems to be experiencing some mission drift as the years go on. Headliners Blink-182 and Pierce The Veil fit the original vision, but the new lineup seems to reflect a broader millennial nostalgia, with late '90s MTV favorites ranging from poppy alt-rockers Third Eye Blind to nu-metal stars Limp Bizkit, with a rather eclectic mix including Michelle Branch, Explosions In The Sky Natasha Bedingfield, Portgual. The Man, Neon Trees, the Psychedelic Furs, 5 Seconds Of Summer, Wheatus, and Ashlee Simpson further down the poster.

In terms of the core WWWY sound, the bill also includes Circa Survive, the Used, Hot Mulligan, Simple Plan, All Time Low, Taking Back Sunday, Sleeping With Sirens, Thrice, Thursday, Bayside, Hawthorne Heights, Saves The Day, From First To Last, State Champs, Story Of The Year, New Found Glory, Senses Fail, the Academy Is..., and more. There are a few more modern heavy hitters like Drain and Die Spitz in the mix too.

WWWY 2027 will take place Oct. 16 at the Las Vegas Festival Grounds. You can sign up for a ticket presale here.

entry.title: Dicky Barrett Shares Statement About His Mighty Mighty Bosstones Revival Without The Rest Of The Band
entry.summary: In 2022, veteran Boston ska-punk band the Mighty Mighty Bosstones broke up in the wake of frontman Dicky Barrett turning into a virulent public anti-vaxxer. So it was a bit of a surprise when the Bosstones were announced for an upcoming Hollywood Bowl show with fellow ska bands Madness, Dance Hall Crashers, Goldfinger, and Reel…
entry.content:
In 2022, veteran Boston ska-punk band the Mighty Mighty Bosstones broke up in the wake of frontman Dicky Barrett turning into a virulent public anti-vaxxer. So it was a bit of a surprise when the Bosstones were announced for an upcoming Hollywood Bowl show with fellow ska bands Madness, Dance Hall Crashers, Goldfinger, and Reel Big Fish. As it turns out, though, it's less a Bosstones reunion, more Dicky Barrett performing Bosstones songs with a bunch of other people.

Shortly after the Bosstones show was announced, fellow ska musician Sammy Kay posted that this version of the Bosstones won't include bassist Joe Gittleman, drummer Joe Sirois, saxophonist Tim "Johnny Vegas" Burton, trombonist Chris Rhodes, or original guitarist Nate Albert. (No word on irreplaceable dancer Ben Carr.) Barrett has a pending trademark on the band name.

On his own Instagram story and the Bosstones' account this morning, Dicky Barrett posted a statement about the current version of the band. He wrote that "5 longtime members" were willing to accept the offer to play with Madness and that "other members have expressed less interest for various reasons." He insists that all of the Bosstones are welcome to return: "This is a positive, good thing. It is with that spirit that I ask any negative energy and hostility be laid to rest." I'm sure that'll do it! Issue resolved! Check out his statement below.

The Bosstones offered no explanation when they announced their breakup five years ago, but Dicky Barrett's public anti-vaxxer stance definitely appears to be a factor. Barrett co-wrote a song with Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. to promote an anti-vaccine rally, and he was fired from his longtime position as Jimmy Kimmel Live! announcer. In a 2022 TNT Radio interview with fellow anti-vaxxer musician Joseph Arthur, Barrett said, "They were uncomfortable, and it ended up the way it ended up... Whatever happened is whatever happened."

entry.title: Miki Berenyi Trio Announce New Album Spoil The Busy Flames: Hear “Expect To Believe”
entry.summary: Miki Berenyi Trio, led by the former Lush singer, have announced new album 'Spoil The Busy Flames' and shared single "Expect To Believe."
entry.content:
Miki Berenyi Trio, the new band led by the former frontwoman of '90s shoegazers Lush, released their debut album Tripla last year. Since then, they've shared two follow-up singles, "Doldrum Days" and "Island Of One." As it turns out, both of those will be on their upcoming sophomore LP Spoil The Busy Flames, which they're officially announcing today.

Spoil The Busy Flames, named after a phrase borrowed from Thomas Hardy's melancholic poem "A Commonplace Day," will be out in February. Alongside the announcement, MB3 have also shared another single entitled "Expect To Believe," a beautifully shimmering, electronic-tinged dream-pop groove that tackles the ironies of living in a post-truth world with a light touch.

"We're exposed to one form of bullshit or another," says lead guitarist/keyboardist KJ "Moose" McKillop. "I don't use social media but for those who do, how do you know what’s real and what you can believe without knowing the source? You're engaging with a world of false consciousness – unreality, half-reality, illusion, insincerity, dogma and anything else that can be categorised as BS." Listen and watch the music video from director Joe Greenwood below.

entry.title: Mil-Spec Dance-Rock Side Project Vivians Release Debut Album Take Your Desires For Reality
entry.summary: Toronto’s crushing, sincere Mil-Spec have consistently been one of the greatest active bands on the hardcore underground for many years, and their various side projects are often really good, too. Last year, for instance, Mil-Spec surprise-released a kickass self-titled EP. A few weeks later, guitarist Dan Darrah released Vacationland, a dreamy and soothing indie rock…
entry.content:
Toronto's crushing, sincere Mil-Spec have consistently been one of the greatest active bands on the hardcore underground for many years, and their various side projects are often really good, too. Last year, for instance, Mil-Spec surprise-released a kickass self-titled EP. A few weeks later, guitarist Dan Darrah released Vacationland, a dreamy and soothing indie rock solo album. So when I tell you that a couple of Mil-Spec members have a new dance-rock band, I expect you to pay attention.

Dan Darrah and his Mil-Spec bandmate Jacob Hellas started the new trio Vivians with Leigh Fisk, from the Toronto shoegaze band Bliss Fields. Their sound is a bright, playful shimmy-shake. It's obviously inspired by the Madchester stuff from the late '80s and early '90s. But unlike most of the Madchester revivalists these days, they're remembered to include the bluesy, countrified guitars that those bands took from the Rolling Stones. I like the bright, airy out-of-time synth-beeps, too.

You like Dazy, right? I hope you do. Vivians' brand-new full-length debut Take Your Desires For Reality has a lot of the same hooky propulsion as Dazy's recent stuff. I'm on my first listen right now, and I'm really into it. Given the track records of everyone involved, this album should not surprise me, but it still does. Hear it for yourself below.

Take Your Desires For Reality is out now on Sunday Drive.

entry.title: Bob Dylan Center Announces “Not Dark Yet,” A 30th Anniversary Time Out Of Mind Tribute Concert
entry.summary: “It’s not dark yet,” Bob Dylan sang. “But it’s gettin’ there.” The year was 1997. Dylan was making a much-heralded comeback with Time Out Of Mind, a bleary and reflective album about aging, death, and the descent into irrelevance. As a middle schooler, I remember hearing about Time Out Of Mind and thinking Dylan, who…
entry.content:
"It's not dark yet," Bob Dylan sang. "But it's gettin' there." The year was 1997. Dylan was making a much-heralded comeback with Time Out Of Mind, a bleary and reflective album about aging, death, and the descent into irrelevance. As a middle schooler, I remember hearing about Time Out Of Mind and thinking Dylan, who was 56 at the time, was impossibly old and craggy. With an album like this one, surely he was nearing the end of the line? Yet 30 years later, he's still here, touring the world, hanging out with the Pope, inspiring cut-for-time SNL sketches about hanging out with the Pope. The man's lived a lot longer and more vigorously than any of us expected, perhaps himself included.

The Bob Dylan Center, the Tulsa-based institution celebrating the good Mr. Zimmerman's life's work, has been throwing some excellent star-studded tribute concerts in recent years. This year they celebrated the 60th(!) anniversary of Blonde On Blonde. The year before, it was the 50th anniversary of Blood On The Tracks. Now it's Time Out Of Mind time.

On Friday, Jan. 29, Cain’s Ballroom will host Not Dark Yet, the Dylan Center's Time Out Of Mind tribute concert. It looks like it will be a hell of a time. Marc Maron will emcee, and Doug Keith will return as music director with a house band including Chatham County Line, brothers Brad and Phil Cook, and Ben Folds Five drummer Darren Jessee. They'll play a Time Out Of Mind set first, then dig into Dylan's catalog for the second set.

Featured performers at the gig will include longtime Dylan collaborator Jim Keltner, Jason Isbell and his former Drive-By Truckers bandmate Patterson Hood (who announced a co-headlining tour today), Elvis Costello, Steve Earle, Margo Price, Diana Krall, Angelique Kidjo, Joe Henry, Ray Benson, Joy Harjo, and one of Dylan's contemporaries from the East Village folk scene of the 1960s, Llewyn Davis. (Alright, fine: Davis is not a real person, but the center did secure the services of Oscar Isaac, the actor who played him, which is almost as impressive as booking a fictional character.)

Keltner, a Tulsa native, will also take part in an onstage conversation and listening session on the night before the show, Thursday, Jan. 28, at the Church Studio. That event is by invitation only for "Not Dark Yet" artists and Bob Dylan Center supporters. Info about how to become such a person, and how to acquire tickets for the big show, is available at the center's website.

entry.content:
Oakland's Still Ruins have a lush, layered take on '80s-style synthpop. They sigh theatrically over expansive keyboard ripples and bright, funky basslines, and they bring up memories of groups like Tears For Fears, ABC, Spandau Ballet, and maybe even Talk Talk. Still Corners started out as a bedroom project in 2018, and they've grown into a touring institution and released a few things, like their self-titled 2024 EP. Now, they're ready to announce their full-length debut.

Early next year. Still Ruins will release their album Through The Glass. The band produced it themselves, and they got Kurt Feldman, the Pains Of Being Pure At Heart drummer and former Depreciation Guild frontman, to mix it. The album-closing single "Armor Of Mourning" is a big, booming, romantic synth-jam that sounds expensive as hell. It would've been right at home on the To Live And Die In LA soundtrack. In a press release, singer Frankie Soto says:

As soon as we finished writing this song, we knew it was going to be the final track on the record. We already wanted it to have a late '80s R&B feel to it, something almost  like Jam and Lewis could have written. "Armor Of Mourning" starts off fairly emotional, but when you get to the end of the track it has the feeling of a final bow and the curtain closing.

Most of us are struggling to be any good at any one fucking thing. I know these different artistic disciplines can be related, but guys like Thomas are…
entry.content:
Alabama native Whitmer Thomas has done really well for himself as an actor and comedian, and he's good at making music, too. Frankly, this seems terribly unfair. Most of us are struggling to be any good at any one fucking thing. I know these different artistic disciplines can be related, but guys like Thomas are making the rest of us look bad. Someone might expect something from us.

A few months ago, Whitmer Thomas released his HBO comedy special Terminal Crew Of Dudes, as well as an accompanying album. I really like the title track, a fired-up country-rock ode to the power of friendship. Next month, Thomas will follow that with Green Room Blues, a new three-song EP that he recorded with past collaborator Melina Duterte, otherwise known as Jay Som.

The EP is supposedly a reflection on show-business life, and that's definitely true of the title track. It's a stripped-down acoustic ballad about being on the road and missing someone back home. I really like the way Thomas writes lyrics: "I want to write something like/ You are the light of my life/ A song to ease your inner cenobite/ A voice memo saying goodnight." Aw. Check it out below.

Katya Urban (vocals/guitar), Ben Ross (bass), Ed Graveline (drums), Sal Huerta (guitar/vocals), and Kiko Torres-Velasco (synth/keys) comprise the LA indie band marguerite. They play artfully dreamy, melody-forward music with a singer-songwriter ethos at its core, weaving notes of slowcore, folk, and ambient into their sonic texture. As of late they do it for Anxiety Blanket Records, a label that has also worked with Draag, Goon, and Coral Grief.

Next year marguerite will release their debut album different life. To introduce it, they're sharing the closing track, a plaintive, poignant beauty called "sofia." Slowly but surely, this one builds to a state of noisy euphoria. Urban's final line gives the album its title: "Am I dreaming that I'm older? Am I dreaming of a different life?" Listen below.

entry.content:
The trio Meiv have a membership that spans national borders and a sound that transcends any and all genre lines. Two longtime collaborators, Tokyo-based Curinus and Hong Kong-based Eugene Nx, started the group, then brought in Eugene's daughter Sara Nx on vocals. The group worked with experimental producer Body Meat on their debut single "Dedeoka," and we posted their Armand Hammer collab "No Future Pt. 1 & 2." Now, Meiv have announced a self-titled debut album full of collaborations.

Body Meat co-produced Meiv's self-titled album. In addition to Armand Hammer, it's got contributions from people like Kassie Krut, By Storm's RiTchie, and Yellow Eyes' Will and Sam Skarstad. Their new single "Acropolis Hill" is a bright, spirited, pretty piece of psychedelic jazz-pop with saxophone from HAIM/Vampire Weekend/Chanel Beads collaborator Henry Solomon. In a press release, the group says:

We think of Meiv as the inside a refrigerator: a futuristic city in anime, the hills of Athens, a forest of confusion, a journey through outer space, a kitschy punk street, a town near the desert, an ice cream city, an otaku laboratory, a deserted shopping mall in the middle of the night, a beachside under the scorching sun.

Illuminating! Below, check out "Acropolis Hill" and the LP's tracklist.

entry.title: Skylar Grey Takes Issue With Olivia Rodrigo & Phoebe Bridgers’ Rock Grammy Nominations
entry.summary: This year’s Grammy nominations came out yesterday, and when my colleague Chris DeVille wrote his instant-reactions column, one of his takeaways was that “genre is over.” Certain big stars have been nominated in categories that might not be their natural homes — Rosalía and Charli XCX in Alternative, Tame Impala in Dance, Olivia Rodrigo and…
entry.content:
This year's Grammy nominations came out yesterday, and when my colleague Chris DeVille wrote his instant-reactions column, one of his takeaways was that "genre is over." Certain big stars have been nominated in categories that might not be their natural homes — Rosalía and Charli XCX in Alternative, Tame Impala in Dance, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers in Rock. Certain artists aren't so happy about this.

The Wisconsin-born singer-songwriter Skylar Grey started off her career as a Linkin Park protege, but she's best known for collaborating with huge artists like Eminem and Dr. Dre. (She co-wrote Eminem's hit Rihanna collab "Love The Way You Lie.") Her most recent solo album Wasted Potential came out earlier this year. Grey has been nominated for her work with other artists a few times in the past, but Wasted Potential didn't get any Grammys attention. The same way that John Summit is mad about how the Grammys define "dance," Grey has some issues with the awards show's version of "rock."

In a social-media video posted after the Grammy nominations came out yesterday, Grey told Alexa, "Play me a song nominated for a Grammy in the rock category." She then shook her head frustratedly when she heard the first few notes of Olivia Rodrigo's Robert Smith duet "What's Wrong With Me" and Phoebe Bridgers' single "Lost Boys," both of which are up for Best Rock Performance. (The other nominees in the category are Angine De Poitrine's "Sarniezz," Geese's Trinidad," and the Rolling Stones' "In The Stars.") Then Grey told Alexa, "Play me the #1 rock song right now" and nodded in satisfaction when she heard "R.I.P.," the recent Motionless In White single that features her.

Grey captioned the video with a note for the Grammys to "do better." During the clip, these words appear onscreen: "Hey Alexa, did the Grammys forget what rock music is?"

First off, that's not how Alexa works. Even if it were, why would someone's personal Amazon assistant be the authority on what rock music is? Grammy voters seem to have difficulty assessing genre, but why would that be any better? And in asking for "the #1 rock song," Grey asked for the rock song currently being played the most on rock radio stations, and that's probably even worse. None of these entities should get to decide these things. Come on.

"R.I.P.," the Motionless In White song that features Skylar Grey, is currently at #1 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Airplay chart. But Olivia Rodrigo is all over the current Billboard rock charts, too. So is Noah Kahan. So what are we doing here?

entry.title: Jason Isbell & Drive-By Truckers Announce Summer Of Joy Tour
entry.summary: Jason Isbell is joining his old band the Drive-By Truckers for a full co-headlining tour next summer dubbed the "Summer Of Joy."
entry.content:
Jason Isbell was a member of the Drive-By Truckers from 2001 to 2007 before going solo and eventually attaining his own roots-rock stardom. He's reunited with his old bandmates a few times over the years, most recently joining DBT to play their classic 2003 album Decoration Day in full at his ShoalsFest in Alabama last month.

As it turns out, that may have been less of a one-off treat and more of a harbinger of things to come, because Isbell and his band the 400 Unit have just announced a big co-headlining tour with Drive-By Truckers next summer. Billed as the "Summer Of Joy," it'll kick off in Nashville on May 6, 2027 and run all the way through Sept. 7 in Tulsa.

A dollar from every ticket sold on the tour will go to Nuçi’s Space, a nonprofit based in Athens, Georgia dedicated to preventing suicide by providing mental health resources and rehearsal and performance space for local musicians. Pre-sale begins tomorrow morning, and general tickets will go on sale Friday, Nov. 20 at 10:00AM. Check out a brief tour announcement video and the full list of dates below.

entry.title: Julien Baker Announces New Album This World Or The Next: Hear “Hound”
entry.summary: We are extremely, magnificently back. Little Oblivions, Julien Baker’s third solo album, came out way back in February 2021. Since then, of course, Baker’s supergroup boygenius released their absolutely massive 2023 album the record, and Baker and Torres also put out the collaborative 2024 queer country LP Send A Prayer My Way. In recent months,…
entry.content:
We are extremely, magnificently back. Little Oblivions, Julien Baker's third solo album, came out way back in February 2021. Since then, of course, Baker's supergroup boygenius released their absolutely massive 2023 album the record, and Baker and Torres also put out the collaborative 2024 queer country LP Send A Prayer My Way. In recent months, Baker has been playing new songs, starting with a Nashville popup gig in September. Now, Baker is finally ready to announce This World Or The Next, their first solo album in six years.

Before Julien Baker released their landmark 2015 solo debut Sprained Ankle, they led a teenage post-hardcore band who were initially known as the Star Killers and who later changed their name to Forrister. For This World Or The Next, Baker reunites with their old Forrister bandmates and longtime friends Matt Gilliam and Calvin Lauber, making music that calls back to their Forrister days. They're getting loud this time.

Baker, Gilliam, and Lauber recorded the self-produced album at the LA studio Lucy's Meat Market. According to a press release, the album's first half is all songs that Baker wrote before heading into the studio. They say, "Hearing the boys jam on them was confirmation. It was so pure." For the songs on the second half, Baker started off with voice memos and drumbeats, and they and their collaborators finished the songs up in the studio. Baker says, "It feels like something we’ve been grasping at for a long time. Making this music, it was like discovering people who spoke your own personal language."

Album opener and lead single "Hound," the first song that Baker wrote for the project, leaves behind the devastating spareness of their past solo albums. It opens with muted piano and acoustic guitar, but it builds into a dramatic churn, putting some serious muscle behind Baker's enormous voice. I bet it'll sound amazing live. Baker still has a few small-venue shows coming up in Seattle, as well as some festival gigs next summer. entry.title: Band To Watch: Awning
entry.summary: “Little Green Book” startled me. Awning’s recent single whisks you away immediately with a brisk, bass-driven backing track and syncopated guitar stabs seemingly stapled in from “Everlong.” The beat is propulsive in a way that reminds me of Radiohead or Tokyo Police Club, but with a swinging swagger you can’t teach and a sense that…
entry.content:
"Little Green Book" startled me. Awning's recent single whisks you away immediately with a brisk, bass-driven backing track and syncopated guitar stabs seemingly stapled in from "Everlong." The beat is propulsive in a way that reminds me of Radiohead or Tokyo Police Club, but with a swinging swagger you can't teach and a sense that it might go off the rails at any moment. And then the chorus hits, and instead of wrecking, the train explodes. Over distortion bombs and droning squall, Christian Dimick shouts with reckless urgency and throat-shredding rawness: "I want to remember what you said! I want to remember every word!" It's one of those holy shit moments rock fans look for, when a band takes it there.

The Auckland rock band's debut album How many angels can dance on the head of a pin? is full of instances like that. Backed by his childhood friend Riley Noonan on drums, Damin McCabe on bass, and Eli Chamberlain and Ethan Broughton on guitar, Dimick lets loose with a fearless volatility to match the music, channeling grief, distress, and elation into anthemic howls and bellows. Even a song like opening track "I'm Up," with its acoustic intro and slo-mo verses, eventually finds its way to clamor. "This is both a love song and a meditation on how life slows down, in a threadbare kind of way, when you are isolated from your loved ones," Dimick says of the song.

Awning are sharing "I'm Up" today along with details on the new album. Set for release on January on Winspear, the project conjures echoes of hard-hitting indie rock from across the decades: the combustible pop acumen of Pixies and their grunge descendants, the ragged rock 'n' roll glory of Divine Fits guys Dan Boeckner and Britt Daniel, the bleary post-punk suaveness of Iceage or King Krule. Dimick, who first found renown as a visual artist, is remarkably good at this rock frontman thing too, and his bandmates feed off each other's energy to powerful effect.

Below, check out "I'm Up" video, read my recent conversation with Dimick, and check out the tracklist for How many angels can dance on the head of a pin?

Awning is promoted as this band from Christian Dimick, an acclaimed visual artist. Is it fair to say you were known for your visual art before your music?

CHRISTIAN DIMICK: I don't really know. I've been playing music since I was a little kid, and I only really started making paintings or drawings after high school. But I don't know what I was known for first.

Tell me about your path as an artist. How did you break through? And what do you feel has been the appeal of your art? What do people tend to notice and appreciate about it?

DIMICK: About both mediums, or…? 

Sure, it can be either one. I meant your visual art, but I'm open to hearing about the music now too.

DIMICK: I think people respond to how I work intuitively in both visual art and music. That's one thing that working with painting and drawing has taught me over the years, spending lots of time in a painting studio on my own, is to trust my own judgment and be confident in when I should hold onto things and when I should let them go, and when an idea is working and when it's not. You're not really surrounded by other people to help you along with making decisions. You have to get very good at making them on your own, and in an immediate fashion. 

Yeah, I think that's something that people respond to. If people have said something really nice to me after the show, it's that. All of us, or the music, or me as a performer, it seems like I'm playing from an immediate space. I don't go on stage and think about what I'm doing. I try to do the exact opposite. It's a space where not having forethought is something that's admired or positive. And it's the same with painting. The more I do it, the easier it becomes to not overthink what I'm doing. And that's something that's been transferred from drawing or painting into music over the years, I think. Being a visual artist has made me a different kind of musician than I was.

You mentioned you did music first? 

DIMICK: When I was a little kid, my granddad, he was a concert violinist. Not as his full-time job, but he played the violin. So when I was a little kid, I learned the violin. And then, when I was about 6, I started learning the guitar as well. And then I played music all through my teenage years, different sort of punk bands. And then I sort of just found my — I was actually studying music, and then became really disenchanted with studying music. So I started painting and drawing all the time, and then I sort of swapped degrees at university, and then spent a bunch of years not really playing much music and more focusing on visual art. And now it's all coming full circle.

Why did you become disenchanted with studying music?

DIMICK: This is when I was maybe 18 or 19. I was studying composition, which was super based in learning a lot of theory and reading music charts, just really theory based, and it felt super uncreative to me. And I think what I really needed at that time was to be going out and playing music with other people. But as someone leaving high school, you feel like you need to go university ‘cause that's what everyone else is doing, so I went and did that and was very unhappy. But I found my own way, and it actually led me to doing something that I really love, that I would never have thought I would have done.

You're an artist peer at the Grace Gallery. What does that mean?

DIMICK: It just means I'm a represented artist by that gallery, and that I'm essentially part of the family. We try and not operate on a traditional model of galleries. It's more like I'm a friend of the gallery as opposed to being a client or whatever of the gallery, if that makes sense.

Is it similar to being signed to a record label or not?

DIMICK: Yeah, I guess there's some similarities there, maybe. With Grace, the gallery I show with, it's a professional relationship. But also my friend Emil [Scheffmann] who runs it, he's my very, very good friend, and it's quite a relaxed professional relationship. Whereas signing on with the label felt a bit more serious and intense. You have to get an entertainment lawyer, and you have to do all this other scary shit. Especially with someone overseas that you haven't met before, it's all a bit more intense. But there's similarities there. You have a loyalty to this person, and they give you opportunities, and then you give them your work. It's a trade-off. There's similarities there for sure.

Speaking of signing to a record label, how did you end up with Winspear?

DIMICK: It was kind of bizarre. I was in Melbourne on a painting residency, and then I met with a friend of a friend called Emma, who's now our manager. Our bass player Damon sent her the record ’cause he knew she worked in music and she might be interested in hearing it and know some people that we could send it to. And then Emma was keen to jump on board to be our manager. So then she started sending the record out to people, and Winspear just picked up the record. We had no expectations as to anyone being interested at all. If you'd asked me at this time last year whether I would have thought this was a possibility, I would have said no for sure. But yeah, Winspear listened to it, they liked it, and then we had a couple of casual Zoom calls online. And Jared [Jones], who runs Winspear, you know, played it very cool and we couldn't really tell if he was, he was interested or not.

And then maybe one month or two months went by, and then they proposed releasing the record through Winspear. And then here we are. And now we've developed a really beautiful friendship with Jared and everyone who works there. They're incredibly nice people, and I feel like we're relatively fresh as a band. People don't really know anything about us. For them to pick up the record and want to work on it with us, just based on how much they like the music, is a big compliment.

Were you familiar with the label before?

DIMICK: I wasn't massively familiar with the label, like as an entity, but I really liked a lot of bands that were on the label that I didn't realize were on Winspear, like Slow Pulp and Teethe. I love those bands, but I'd never really made a connection or focused in on them as a label. Until all of this stuff happened, I've never really been a label person.

You're not following along like, “Oh, this artist’s on this label.”

DIMICK: No, unless it's like — you know, we have Flying Nun here in New Zealand. Maybe I'm making myself look bad, but I've only really deep-dived into Flying Nun's whole discography. But I've been more interested in labels since all this has happened.

Yeah, it's suddenly become very personally relevant.

DIMICK: Yeah, totally. You can see a label's taste. When you start sifting through all their artists, you can see all these threads between groups or artists.

Your bio talks about 2023 as the launch of this version of the band with the five of you. Did Awning exist in some other form before that?

DIMICK: Awning before that was just me in a shed, making demos on my laptop. But yeah, eventually me and some friends decided it would be fun to play some shows. So we put a lineup together, and Riley [Noonan], who still plays drums, was playing drums, and Eli [Chamberlain] was in it. And our friend Baxter [Perry] at the time was playing bass, and our friend Tharushi [Bowatte]. And then the lineup changed. I moved cities. But yeah, we started playing as a band in around 2023. It became more of an actual thing as opposed to me just on my own.

How did the music change when you became this full-fledged band? Was the style pretty much the same when it was just you?

DIMICK: No, when it was just me, it was very lo-fi, folky.  I was listening to a lot of the Microphones or whatever, or Elliott Smith or something. And then slowly over time, the band’s become louder. Maybe a little bit more abrasive. Just less folky, less acoustic guitars.

Yeah, I was going to say, even compared to the self-titled release you put out last year, this new one seems a lot rawer and heavier to me. What was driving that change?

DIMICK: As each record or release has gone on, it's been more and more writing together in a room as a band. So you're just responding to each other's energy, you're playing in a louder space, or just playing generally louder. So vocals get more intense to match that energy. The songwriting just takes on — it’s a different life force. The way you write a song in a bedroom on your own is so different to writing in a space with other bodies and other people. It’s active, and you're responding to each other. That's why this, the newest record, sounds far more raw. It's just a different setup. 

Did you know your voice could do that before you were writing these songs? It sounds pretty cool.

DIMICK: Not really. Yeah, I think that's another thing, with vocal performance, you're never gonna do that sitting alone in your bedroom. So yeah, sometimes I surprise myself. Like I didn't know I could sing in that register or something. But you just figure out that you can, I guess. So that's one way that the music has evolved.

How do you feel like you've grown as a songwriter since you started this project?

DIMICK: I think I've become better at working alongside people. Like the band as it's developed into this upcoming release, I feel like over the years, just in general I've gotten better at writing music with other people and being a better listener as a musician. I think you just pick stuff up through doing or through osmosis or whatever. I couldn't really tell you a specific thing, but I know that I've gotten more confident. And like I was saying earlier, a little bit more trusting in my ideas, and when they're shit and when they're OK. I don't really know if I've gotten better as a musician or anything, but I think I've learned to trust my songwriting intuition a bit more. I'd say maybe that I've gotten a bit better at that.

When you put out “Little Green Book,” you said it was about a grief too heavy to sing about in a song. Is it too heavy to speak about in an interview?

DIMICK: Yeah, maybe, if that's alright. I think that that's the purpose of the music. It's a way to express something in a cathartic public way. It's too uncomfortable to do that in any other format. It's a way to be expressive without giving people your life story. Not everyone needs to know about that, your private business. It’s good to keep something for you, I think.

That's cool, but I will say there are some other songs on the album that are a little less abstract. Like that song is sandwiched by “I'm Up” and “Play Dumb,” and I feel like those are really straightforward and relatable, almost universal.

DIMICK: Totally. Yeah, I agree.

I get what you're saying about trying to put a degree of separation in, but some of these songs have a plainspokenness about what you're feeling that makes it really easy to latch onto. I think some writers maybe would try to use more oblique language, but it feels like you're giving somebody a lot to latch onto in terms of putting themselves in the song. “Play Dumb” is a song I can imagine a lot of people shouting along to.

DIMICK: Yeah, I hear what you're saying. I think for certain songs about certain things, there's that necessity to create some distance through the style of language you're using within the lyrics. And then there's some songs where it feels OK and it feels like people would actually quite easily relate to your experience, so it feels OK to be direct in the way you write the lyrics. It just varies between subject.

“how many angels can dance on the head of a pin?” Where does that song come from, and why is it the title track?

DIMICK: That song is kind of a multitude of things. It's about a dream I had about my mum who passed away when I was a kid. And I've only had a select few dreams about her in my life. But the lyrics in the verse are taken from the imagery of that dream. And then I guess the question or the statement that is the chorus lyric is more reflective of my life currently. That statement essentially means, “How many more arguments can one have with themselves before we can get on with it?” When you merge those two things together, it's kind of strange, but it works for me. A lot of it's imagery taken from a dream.

I'm sorry to hear about your mom. I imagine that probably hangs over a lot of what you create.

DIMICK: Yeah, definitely. You're talking about universal things; at some point, everyone will experience this sort of thing. It's a universal thing. People stick around, or the idea of people floats around, and they affect what you make, especially as an artist. Some people say people with strong creative antennae are maybe a little bit more curious and interested in making a connection with people that aren't here. I definitely feel like that sometimes.

entry.title: Ryley Walker Announces New Album Darkening The Glass: Hear “Cloud Of Beaujolais”
entry.summary: Ryley Walker is on the move, both musically and geographically. The Illinois native and longtime NYC fixture recently relocated to Los Angeles, just in time to roll out a new album that completely reinvents his sound. Walker surprised us in September by returning with “Carrier,” a radical stylistic departure that found the guitar experimentalist and…
entry.content:
Ryley Walker is on the move, both musically and geographically. The Illinois native and longtime NYC fixture recently relocated to Los Angeles, just in time to roll out a new album that completely reinvents his sound.

Walker surprised us in September by returning with "Carrier," a radical stylistic departure that found the guitar experimentalist and prog/jazz/psych-folk singer-songwriter delving into heavy distortion and avant-garde electronics. It suggested Walker's new partnership with the AD 93 label would take him into new creative pastures. Today we learn more about this new era.

Walker has announced Darkening The Glass, his first new album since 2021's excellent Course In Fable. It's coming in February, and besides "Carrier," it includes today's new single "Cloud Of Beaujolais." Walker recorded it at the Sweat Loge in his former home base of Chicago. To give you a sense of the album's direction, he's credited with vocals, guitar, computer, loops, recording, samples, programming, electronics, and synths.

The new approach was learned from of Ben Kudler of Computer Music For Dorks and Radical Democracy, who reportedly schooled Walker in the ways of laptop music. Kudler contributes to the new tracks, as do Andrew Scott Young (double bass/fretless bass), Bill MacKay (guitar), Max Allison (drum programming), and producer Cooper Crain (who played synths in addition to recording and mixing).

Compared to "Carrier," new single "Cloud Of Beaujolais" is not as jarringly different from Walker's past work. The jazzy post-rock Jim O'Rourke guitar tapestries are prevalent, and Walker's low-register ruminations greet us like a sad, thoughtful old friend. Yet electronic shrapnel blows through the landscape at times, blending with orchestral strings to ensure you never know what's coming next. I love the last verse: "A tasteless mother tongue/ The Midwest dialect/ The slang of retail workers/ Saying, 'Fuck this,' with their chests."

Walker's words on the track:

This was the last tune written for the record. I sat in a chair with my forehead on the kitchen counter for the whole afternoon while I fleshed it out. I got a big line on my forehead and everybody kept asking, "What’s wrong with your forehead?" I said it was eczema because I didn’t want to admit I’d written a song. A pretty inept feeling. Andrew Young and Bill MacKay play beautifully on this.

Listen below.

entry.title: Danzig Guitarist John Christ Dead At 61
entry.summary: John Christ, lead guitarist for Danzig during that band’s classic era, has passed away. On Monday night, Christ’s Instagram announced that the guitarist died on Nov. 15, adding, “No services are planned and we kindly ask everyone to respect the family’s privacy during this time.” No cause of death has been reported, but Christ had…
entry.content:
John Christ, lead guitarist for Danzig during that band's classic era, has passed away. On Monday night, Christ's Instagram announced that the guitarist died on Nov. 15, adding, "No services are planned and we kindly ask everyone to respect the family's privacy during this time." No cause of death has been reported, but Christ had been suffering from an unspecified health issue in recent months. Christ was 61.

John Christ was born John Wolfgang Knoll, and he grew up in the Baltimore suburb of Catonsville. For kids in Baltimore during Danzig's initial reign, it was unbelievably cool to know that the band's resident guitar hero was a guy from the area. Christ started playing guitar as a kid, and he studied classical guitar at the Peabody Institute and jazz at Towson State University. In 1987, he dropped out of college to join Glenn Danzig's post-Misfits band Samhain, which was about to evolve into the band known as Danzig. He secured his spot in the band by calling Glenn Danzig up multiple times and playing guitar solos on his answering machine.

Samhain had already played their final show under that name when Christ joined up, though he did play guitar on their album Final Descent, which didn't come out until 1990. Rick Rubin wanted to sign the band, and he convinced them to change their name to just Danzig, reflecting the group's changing lineup and direction. Christ and former Black Flag drummer Chuck Biscuits joined the band, which continued to feature Glenn Danzig and Samhain bassist Eerie Von. They made their debut on the Rubin-produced Less Than Zero soundtrack in 1986, releasing the relatively conventional rocker "You And Me (Less Than Zero)" under the name Glenn Danzig & The Power And Fury Orchestra.

In 1988, Rick Rubin left Def Jam, the label he co-founded, to start his new imprint Def American, which later changed its name to American Recordings. The first album to come out on Def American was Danzig's Rubin-produced self-titled debut. The album opened with Christ's elemental riff for "Twist Of Cain," still one of the all-time great triumphant, horns-up metal guitar lines. As the band name implies, the focus of Danzig was Glenn Danzig's simmering charisma and caveman-Elvis howl. But Christ's sinister, bottom-heavy guitar was a key element, and he looked cool as hell shredding shirtlessly in those videos.

Danzig were essentially a cult band, though their self-titled debut eventually went gold. They toured with bands like Metallica and Slayer, and they continued to crank out titanic-sounding records backed with nasty-ass John Christ riffs. Danzig's next two albums, 1990's Danzig II: Lucifuge and 1992's Danzig III: How The Gods Kill, were arguably as strong as the debut, and Christ did champion-level work on songs like "Her Black Wings" and "Dirty Black Summer." The 1993 EP Thrall-Demonsweatlive included a live version of "Mother," a song from Danzig's debut, that became a surprise hit, reaching #43 on the Billboard Hot 100.

Danzig's industrial-influenced 1994 album 4 wasn't as successful as the band hoped. John Christ parted ways with Danzig in 1995, citing disagreements with Glenn Danzig. He never rejoined, and the band never recaptured the magic of their early records. Christ released the 1999 solo album Flesh Caffeine, played on a 2001 Metallica tribute album, and did soundtrack work for TV networks. He suffered debilitating injuries in a 1994 car crash, and it took him years to regain his guitar skills

On his Instagram a few months ago, Christ wrote, "Recently, I have been focusing on a medical issue that has been kicking my butt and I am in the process of recuperating. The doctors have requested that I take a few months off to rest up and let my body get back to normal or else they said they will send Glenn to my house to babysit — that is motivation enough to get better!" Check out some of Christ's work below.
